1373.title: The Divine Mercy chaplet
1373.hook: on rosary beads: eternal Father, I offer you, and for the sake of his sorrowful passion
1373.howItsDone: Catholics who keep the Divine Mercy devotion pray the chaplet on ordinary rosary beads, alone or in groups, often at three in the afternoon and especially around Divine Mercy Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, devotion: freely chosen, growing around the liturgy and leading back to it. Your line was optional, and loved.

A string of beads with a small crucifix at the end. Anyone would call it a rosary, and it is. But the prayer moving through it today is not the rosary. Someone holding those beads on a bus whispers one short line on each small bead: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. Same beads, a different prayer. Saint Faustina recorded it in her diary, and it's now prayed far from her convent.
screen: `THE SAME BEADS.` → `A DIFFERENT PRAYER.` → `HAVE MERCY ON US AND ON THE WHOLE WORLD.`

segments.voice: It's built from two movements that take turns. First, an offering. On each large bead, the person praying speaks to God the Father: eternal Father, I offer you. What's offered is Christ himself, his body and blood, soul and divinity, for our sins and those of the whole world. That's a bold thing to say at a kitchen table. It echoes the Mass, where the Church offers Christ to the Father; here, one person with beads joins it in a small way. Second, the asking. On each small bead, the same line: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. The reason given isn't the person's own goodness. It's Christ's suffering. In Luke, Jesus tells of a man who prays in that spirit. A tax collector stands far back in the Temple, won't lift his eyes, strikes his breast, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list of achievements. Just the request. And it never asks mercy for me alone. It's us, and the whole world: the driver, the stranger across the aisle, the people in the news you can't stand. The chaplet closes by calling God holy, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, and asking once more for mercy. Those titles echo an old hymn of the Eastern churches called the Trisagion, the thrice-holy. So a prayer recorded by a Polish sister ends on words the East has long sung. People pray it alone, in groups, at bedsides, and at three in the afternoon, which is tomorrow's story.
screen: `FIRST, AN OFFERING TO THE FATHER.` · `THEN, THE ASKING.` · `US, AND THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `IT ENDS ON THE THRICE-HOLY.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Hold beads if you have them; if not, your fingers will do. If you pray, say the whole chaplet as a prayer card or your parish gives it, or take only the short line, have mercy on us and on the whole world, slowly, a few times. Each time, let a different face come to mind: someone close, someone far away, someone hard to love.
The Divine Mercy chaplet. A short prayer on rosary beads, recorded by Saint Faustina: Christ offered to the Father, and mercy asked for us and the whole world.
Your line: have mercy on us. That us leaves no one out. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1374.title: Three o'clock
1374.hook: the hour of Christ's death, kept as an hour of mercy
1374.howItsDone: Some Catholics pause at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition gives for Jesus's death, to pray the Divine Mercy chaplet or simply to remember the cross; religious communities pray the mid-afternoon hour of the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Mercy chaplet: an offering to the Father, and a plea for the whole world. Your line was have mercy on us.

In Acts, Peter and John are walking up to the Temple in the middle of the afternoon. Not to preach, but to pray, at an hour set aside for it. At the gate, a man who has never walked asks them for money. The same hour turns up in the Gospels, on an afternoon when, Mark says, darkness covered the land. And some Catholics still mark it, by the clock, every day.
screen: `PETER AND JOHN GO UP TO PRAY.` → `AN HOUR SET ASIDE.` → `STILL MARKED BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Gospels count the day's hours from morning, so their ninth hour falls in the middle of the afternoon, and Catholic tradition keeps it at three. Acts says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer." An hour of prayer, already, before it meant anything more. Mark tells of darkness over the land from the sixth hour until the ninth, and places Jesus's death at the ninth. Luke gives his last words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Then he breathes his last. For Christians, the afternoon hour of prayer became the hour he died. The Church's own prayer kept the hour. The Liturgy of the Hours has a short mid-afternoon office called None, the ninth. Monks and sisters stop their work for it; so do some lay people with a prayer book in a desk drawer. Then the hour of mercy. In her diary, Faustina wrote that Jesus asked her to honor the hour of his death, at three o'clock, and to ask then for mercy, especially for sinners. She records that even a brief moment was enough: a thought of the cross while carrying on with her work. So in some Catholic hospitals and parishes, a bell or a voice marks three. Some people pray the chaplet then. Some pause for a few seconds at a desk, in traffic, in a checkout line. None of it is required. That's the shape of a devotion: an ordinary minute of an ordinary afternoon, turned toward one afternoon on a hill outside Jerusalem.
screen: `THE NINTH HOUR: MID-AFTERNOON.` · `THE HOUR JESUS DIED.` · `NONE: THE CHURCH'S AFTERNOON PRAYER.` · `FAUSTINA: THE HOUR OF MERCY.` · then, large: `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Think of where you'll be at three this afternoon, a desk, a kitchen, a car, and choose one tiny sign for that moment: setting down whatever's in your hands, one slow breath, the sign of the cross. If you pray, borrow Jesus's words from Luke, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit, or ask mercy for someone who's suffering; if you don't, let three o'clock be a moment to remember that person.

1375.title: First Fridays
1375.hook: nine first Fridays of confession and communion, from the Sacred Heart devotion
1375.howItsDone: Catholics who keep the First Friday devotion go to Mass and receive communion on the first Friday of the month, often after confession, in honor of the Sacred Heart; some keep nine in a row, and parishes often add confessions and adoration that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three o'clock: an hour of prayer that became the hour Jesus died. Your line was the hour of mercy.

A parish bulletin, near the bottom, between the bake sale and a reminder about parking: First Friday. Confessions before the morning Mass. Adoration afterward. Some people circle it. Some keep a small card in a wallet with boxes to tick, month after month, until the boxes run out. It's a devotion with a number built into it, and a promise attached to the number.
screen: `FIRST FRIDAY: CONFESSIONS, MASS.` → `BOXES TO TICK.` → `A NUMBER AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: It begins in a convent in France, with a nun this path has met before, Margaret Mary Alacoque. In her account, Jesus showed her his heart and asked that people receive communion on the first Friday of each month, in reparation: making up, in love, for the coldness his love so often meets. Why Friday? The Gospels place the crucifixion on the day of preparation before the Sabbath, the day Christians call Friday. Every Friday echoes Good Friday, and the first of each month became a small Good Friday on the calendar. Then the promise. In a letter, Margaret Mary passed on what's known as the great promise: that those who received communion on the first Friday for nine months in a row would not die without the grace of repentance and the sacraments. That's where the nine comes from. The Church has permitted the devotion and encouraged it. It doesn't teach that nine Fridays work like a ticket; in Catholic teaching, grace is never bought by keeping a schedule. What the day holds: the devotion asks for communion, and the Church asks anyone aware of serious sin to go to confession before communion. So parishes open the confessional that morning. Some add an hour of adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, or a litany of the Sacred Heart. In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." A first Friday is an appointment with that invitation. Nine of them, one a month, is a long time to keep showing up. That's part of the point.
screen: `MARGARET MARY: COMMUNION, IN REPARATION.` · `FRIDAY ECHOES GOOD FRIDAY.` · `NINE IN A ROW: THE GREAT PROMISE.` · `CONFESSION, COMMUNION, ADORATION.` · then, large: `I WILL REFRESH YOU.`

segments.voice: Find, in your head or on your phone, the first Friday of next month, and mark it: a dot, a star, a word. If you're Catholic and you pray, you might plan to go to Mass that morning, or to confession, or simply stop into a church for a few minutes. If that isn't your practice, the day can still carry something: an hour kept free, one kindness for someone who's worn out.

1376.title: The Sacred Heart at home
1376.hook: families place an image of the Sacred Heart in the home
1376.howItsDone: Some Catholic families enthrone an image of the Sacred Heart in a central room of the house, usually with a blessing by a priest and a family act of consecration, and renew it on the feast of the Sacred Heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, First Fridays: communion in reparation, nine months running, a promise attached. Your line was nine fridays.

"Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock." That's Christ speaking in the Bible's last book, the one the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse, and the next line says what happens if someone opens. Some Catholic families take that line almost literally. They hang a picture where the family actually lives and invite him in, on purpose, with a small ceremony.
screen: `I STAND AT THE GATE, AND KNOCK.` → `A PICTURE ON THE WALL.` → `AN INVITATION, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The practice has a formal name: enthronement. A family chooses a picture or statue of the Sacred Heart, Jesus pointing to his heart, and gives it a place of honor: the living room, the kitchen wall, above the table. Not a closet, not a hallway nobody uses. It's meant to be seen in the ordinary traffic of family life. A priest may come to bless the image. The family gathers, prays together, and consecrates the household to the Sacred Heart: a promise to treat Christ as the head of the home. Some families sign a certificate, hang it nearby, and renew the consecration each year on the feast. Tradition links all this to Margaret Mary, who wrote that Jesus promised to bless the places where an image of his heart is set up and honored. The full verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." To sup is to eat supper. So the picture isn't decoration, and it isn't a guard dog. It's a reminder that a guest has been invited to the table: to the arguments, the homework, the overdue bills, the birthday cake. Last, what it asks of the household. Hanging an image is easy. Living under it is harder. The hope is that the picture works quietly over time: a sharp word swallowed because he's looking; a short grace before a meal that used to be eaten standing at the counter. One glance at the wall says it: he lives here.

segments.voice: If there's a Sacred Heart picture or any holy image in your home, stand before it, or bring it to mind, and look at it as if for the first time. If you pray, make the sign of the cross toward it and ask God to bless everyone who walks past it. If there's no image, think about where one would go: the room where your household really lives, not the room that's tidy.

1377.title: Novenas
1377.hook: nine days of prayer, after the apostles waiting for the Spirit
1377.howItsDone: Catholics pray novenas, nine consecutive days of prayer, before feasts such as Christmas, for particular needs, for the dead, or asking a saint's intercession; parishes sometimes hold public novenas with a prayer service each evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sacred Heart at home: a guest invited to supper where the family really lives. Your line was he lives here.

What would you keep doing for nine days straight, for someone else? A woman's brother is having surgery next week. Her aunt hands her a folded leaflet: a short prayer, the same each day, nine days of it. Start tonight, the aunt says, and you'll finish before he goes in. She has never done anything like it and isn't sure what it will do. But nine days is something she can hold in her hands.
screen: `NINE DAYS, FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `A FOLDED LEAFLET.` → `START TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: A novena is nine days of prayer, for one intention or to prepare for a feast. The prayer can be short and the same each day, or a new reflection daily. What makes it a novena is the shape: nine days, kept one after another. Tradition traces that shape to the apostles. In Acts, before he ascends, Jesus tells them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father. So they wait, and pray, and the Spirit comes at Pentecost. Tradition counts that waiting as nine days and calls it the first novena; that's tomorrow's story. There are many kinds. Some novenas prepare for a feast, like Christmas or a saint's day. Some ask for something: work, healing, a safe birth. Some are for someone who has just died. Some ask a saint to pray alongside. A novena isn't a vending machine: nine coins in, one answer out. Some leaflets promise that a certain novena never fails. The Church doesn't teach that; the Catechism warns against treating any prayer as if its power came from saying it correctly. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens. For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard." What does it do? It brings a person back to the same intention day after day, long after the first rush of worry has faded. Day one is easy. Day six, when nothing seems to be happening, may be where the real praying starts. Nine days is practice in waiting, the way the apostles waited, without knowing when or how the answer will come.

If you don't, keep the shape anyway: one minute a day, for nine days, holding that person in mind.

1378.title: The Pentecost novena
1378.hook: the first novena, from Ascension to Pentecost
1378.howItsDone: Between the Ascension and Pentecost, some Catholics and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit, often using the words come, Holy Spirit, or the hymns that begin with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was novena: nine days, one after another, practice in waiting. Your line was nine days.

The friends of Jesus are walking back into Jerusalem from the hill called Olivet. A short walk. He's gone from their sight, in a way none of them can explain, and before he went he told them to wait. Not to preach yet, not to organize, not to scatter. Wait. So they climb the stairs to an upper room and do the one thing they've been asked to do. Nobody tells them how long it will take.
screen: `BACK FROM OLIVET.` → `HE TOLD THEM TO WAIT.` → `UP THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: Acts lists who's in the room, name by name: Peter and John, James and Andrew, and the rest. Then it adds more, in the Douay-Rheims: "All these were persevering with one mind in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren." So what tradition calls the first novena was not one person alone with a leaflet. It was a room full of people: women, unnamed here, Jesus's family, his mother. Persevering, with one mind, in prayer, they wait for something they've been promised and can't produce themselves. Then the end of the waiting. Acts two opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place." Pentecost was already a Jewish feast, the harvest feast Jews still keep as Shavuot, which is why the city is crowded with pilgrims. Then comes a sound from heaven like a mighty wind, tongues like fire, and the Spirit. Notice where it finds them: all together. Tradition counts the days from the Ascension to Pentecost as nine, and keeps them as a novena to the Holy Spirit. Pope Leo the Thirteenth, in a letter on the Holy Spirit, asked the whole Church to make that novena every year, and some parishes still mark it. One prayer used is just three words: Come, Holy Spirit. They open an old hymn and a well-worn prayer, and they say exactly what the upper room was doing. Waiting together is different from waiting alone. Someone else keeps the vigil when you nod off.

1379.title: Medals and scapulars
1379.hook: sacramentals, not charms: they only help if they lead to faith
1379.howItsDone: Some Catholics wear a blessed medal or a scapular, often received at baptism, first communion or confirmation, as a sign of faith and a reminder to pray; the Church teaches these are sacramentals and warns against treating them as charms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pentecost novena: praying with one mind until the Spirit came. Your line was waiting together.

A tray at a flea market, under scratched glass: tiny oval medals, tarnished, some on broken chains. A saint holding a cross and a book. A woman with rays streaming from her open hands. Each one hung around somebody's neck once, through a first communion, a deployment, a long illness. Now they sit beside old keys and buttons. They look like lucky charms. The Church insists they're not.
screen: `A TRAY OF OLD MEDALS.` → `ONCE AROUND SOMEONE'S NECK.` → `CHARMS? THE CHURCH SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Medals and scapulars are sacramentals: blessed signs that point past themselves. The Catechism says they don't work the way sacraments do. They prepare a person to receive grace and to cooperate with it, through the prayer of the Church. A medal is a small image struck in metal: a saint, Mary, the cross. The one with rays streaming from Mary's hands is called the Miraculous Medal; tradition says Mary showed its design to a young sister in Paris. A scapular, as this path saw earlier in the year, is a religious habit shrunk to two small panels of cloth, worn front and back as a sign of belonging. Then the line the Church draws. Superstition, the Catechism says, includes treating a sign's power as if it came from the outward act alone, apart from the heart of the person using it. A medal trusted like a rabbit's foot, by someone who never turns toward God, has become exactly what the Church warns against. In Ephesus, Acts says, some traveling exorcists, sons of a man named Sceva, watch Paul heal in the name of Jesus, and try to use that name like a formula: we command you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches. The evil spirit answers: Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you? And it overpowers them. The name wasn't a password. It belonged to a relationship they didn't have. So what is a medal for? It's a reminder you can touch. Fingers find it during a meeting, a medical scan, a bumpy flight, and the heart gets pointed back toward God and toward a saint who stands for something: courage, purity, care for travelers. The metal doesn't hold the grace. It holds the memory.
screen: `SACRAMENTALS: SIGNS THAT POINT PAST THEMSELVES.` · `A MEDAL, A SCAPULAR.` · `THE NAME WAS NOT A PASSWORD.` · `IT HOLDS THE MEMORY, NOT THE GRACE.` · then, large: `NOT A CHARM.`

segments.voice: If you have a medal, a cross or a scapular, hold it; if not, think of one worn by someone you love. Ask what it stands for: which saint, which promise, who gave it. If you pray, hold it and offer the day to God; if you don't, let it be a small weight that remembers for you.
Medals and scapulars. Small blessed signs, of metal or cloth, worn as reminders of faith and belonging. Sacramentals, not charms: they help only when they lead to faith.
